articles.title: Optical Tech Would Update a Robot’s AI on the Fly
articles.summary: Cornell Tech researchers demonstrated an optical receiver that can directly alter chip memory using QR-code-like light patterns, potentially enabling AI model parameters to be updated with less energy than conventional electrical memory links. The approach targets a major AI hardware bottleneck: moving large model data between DRAM and processors, with possible future uses in data centers, self-driving cars, edge AI, and robotics. The technology remains early-stage, with commercialization challenges including larger photosensitive SRAM cells and the need for high-speed optical transmitters.
articles.advisor_relevance: This article highlights that AI scaling is not only about compute, but also about memory bandwidth, energy use, and data movement. While the specific technology is far from commercialization, it reinforces the investment relevance of AI infrastructure bottlenecks and potential second-derivative opportunities in memory, interconnects, optical communication, and edge AI hardware.

articles.title: How AI is shortening drug discovery timelines in China
articles.summary: Insilico Medicine says its AI-assisted drug discovery workflow has shortened some preclinical candidate nomination timelines to about one year, with its fastest program reaching nomination in nine months versus roughly four-and-a-half years for conventional approaches. The company combines generative AI for target identification and molecule design with laboratory validation in China, where infrastructure, costs, and regulatory pathways may accelerate development. Its AI-designed drug Rentosertib is moving toward a Phase III trial in China, though later-stage success rates for AI-designed drugs remain unproven.
articles.advisor_relevance: This is a concrete example of AI moving beyond software demos into physical R&D workflows, with potential implications for biotech productivity, contract research activity, and pharmaceutical development economics. The article also highlights China as a faster and lower-cost drug development hub, while reminding investors that early discovery speed does not yet prove higher clinical success or faster commercialization.
